data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["In finance, returns are continuous and quantitative; in judgment, outcomes are often binary.","Financial models assume rational actors; human panel members are subject to social dynamics and shared biases."],"overturn_conditions":["The expert's intuition is demonstrably superior on items where the panel exhibits high disagreement.","The panel's disagreement is not predictive of error, suggesting it is not epistemically informative."],"shared_structure":["Both involve a portfolio of independent bets (judgments).","Both rely on the independence of errors to achieve a better expected outcome than a single bettor.","Both require that the variance of the individual bets be informative about the quality of the portfolio."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_002","SRC_005"],"transfer_claims":["The 'diversification benefit' is genuine only if the assets are truly independent. If the panel's errors are correlated (e.g., by a flawed checklist), the benefit is illusory.","The 'tracking error' is the diagnostic: if the portfolio (panel) tracks the benchmark (checklist) perfectly but fails to outperform in risk-adjusted terms (calibrated uncertainty), it's mere compliance."]},"claim":"The panel's reliability gain is genuine if and only if the panel's collective judgment on checklist items demonstrates calibrated redundancy\u2014specifically, if higher panel disagreement on a specific checklist item predicts a higher probability of an incorrect final answer, and this disagreement-accuracy correlation is stronger than the expert's self-reported confidence-accuracy correlation. This distinguishes genuine gain from mere compliance because 'mere compliance' implies mechanical adherence regardless of item difficulty, whereas genuine reliability implies the panel's uncertainty is epistemically informative.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The checklist forces a binary choice on each item, eliminating the possibility of calibrated redundancy.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The expert's intuition is already well-calibrated, making the panel's redundancy signal no more informative.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"Panel disagreement is driven by personality clashes rather than task difficulty.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Genuine reliability is not just about getting the right answer; it's about *knowing when you don't know*. A panel that merely complies with a checklist will produce answers with uniformly high confidence (because the checklist is followed). A panel that has genuinely internalized the task's logic will exhibit calibrated uncertainty: members will disagree on hard items, and this disagreement will be predictive of errors. If this internal signal of difficulty is present and more reliable than the expert's gut feeling, the reliability gain is genuine, not merely procedural.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
